advances:
Every actual canonical counterexample in the all-double positive-middle branch has a unique dominant \(Q\)-cap. After relabeling it as \(x_1=q_{23}\), the index \(1\) uniquely minimizes the sharpened Scott quantities \(u_i+m-x_i\), and
\[
x_1>\frac{5m}{9},\qquad
\max\{x_2,x_3\}<\frac{4m}{9},\qquad
x_1-u_1>\frac{5m}{9}.
\]
This gives strict dominant-index bounds for \(c_1\) and \(K\cap\{f_1\geq0\}\), and places the centroid of \(A_2\) in the strict interior of the exact cell \(Q_{23}\). The conclusion is for an actual counterexample and makes no closure claim.
author: /root/mp_r58_scott_ratio_region
external_sources:
P. R. Scott, "On the union of convex bodies with no interior point in common", Mathematika 37 (1990), 245-250, DOI https://doi.org/10.1112/S0025579300012961. The theorem states that if \(K_1,\ldots,K_{d+1}\) are \(d\)-dimensional convex bodies whose interiors have no common point, then
\[
\left|\bigcup_{i=1}^{d+1}K_i\right|
\geq
\frac{(d+1)^d}{(d+1)^d-d^d}\min_i|K_i|.
\]
For \(d=2\), the coefficient is \(9/5\). Accepted fact `aee01fb887f2b3bd` verifies for the present \(K_i=K\cap\{f_i\geq0\}\) that every \(K_i\) is two-dimensional, that the three interiors have no common point, and that their union is contained in \(K\). Thus Scott's theorem applies with planar Lebesgue area.

The planar Grünbaum theorem used through accepted fact `2f9be517307232c7` states: if \(A\subseteq\mathbb R^2\) is a convex body with centroid \(g\), then every closed halfplane \(H\) containing \(g\) satisfies
\[
|A\cap H|\geq\frac49|A|.
\]
The primary source is Branko Grünbaum, "Partitions of mass-distributions and of convex bodies by hyperplanes", Pacific Journal of Mathematics 10 (1960), no. 4, 1257-1261, https://msp.org/pjm/1960/10-4/pjm-v10-n4-p18-p.pdf. Here \(A=A_2\) is a two-dimensional convex body, \(g=g_2\), and the contrary assumption would make \(A_2\cap\{f_1\leq-L_1\}\) a closed halfplane section containing \(g_2\), so every hypothesis is satisfied.
proof:
Accepted fact `aee01fb887f2b3bd` proves that the three convex bodies
\[
K_i=K\cap\{f_i\geq0\}
\]
satisfy Scott's hypotheses, that their union is contained in \(K\), and that
\[
|K_i|=k-c_i.
\]
Under all-double support, \(v_i=m-x_i\). The crossing equality therefore gives the exact identity
\[
|K_i|=k-h+u_i+m-x_i.
\]
Keeping the \(u_i\)-term in Scott's estimate yields
\[
k\geq\frac95\min_i|K_i|
=\frac95\left(k-h+\min_i(u_i+m-x_i)\right).
\]
Rearranging and substituting \(9h=2(M+m+k)\) proves (1).

Now (1) and (2) give
\[
\min_i(u_i+m-x_i)<\frac{4m}{9}.
\tag{12}
\]
Choose an index \(i\) attaining this minimum. Since \(u_i\geq0\), (12) gives
\[
m-x_i<\frac{4m}{9},
\]
and hence
\[
x_i>\frac{5m}{9}.
\tag{13}
\]
Because \(q,x_1,x_2,x_3\) are all positive and
\[
x_1+x_2+x_3=m-q<m,
\]
two different \(x_i\) cannot both exceed \(5m/9\). Thus the index in (13) is unique. Relabel it as \(1\). Then
\[
q+x_2+x_3=m-x_1<\frac{4m}{9},
\]
which proves all of (3).

For \(i=2,3\), (3) gives
\[
u_i+m-x_i\geq m-x_i>\frac{5m}{9}.
\tag{14}
\]
On the other hand, the minimum in (12) is below \(4m/9\). Hence neither \(2\) nor \(3\) can minimize, and \(1\) is the unique minimizing Scott index. In particular,
\[
u_1+m-x_1<\frac{4m}{9},
\]
which rearranges to (4). Subtracting (4) from \(x_1\) gives (5).

Under all-double support, the only positive \(Q\)-cell omitting \(1\) is \(Q_{23}\), so
\[
v_1=m-x_1.
\]
The crossing at index \(1\) therefore gives
\[
c_1=h-u_1-v_1
=h-u_1-m+x_1
=h-m+t_1.
\]
Together with (5), this proves (6). Accepted fact `aee01fb887f2b3bd` audits the exact boundary convention:
\[
\left|K\cap\{f_1\geq0\}\right|=k-c_1.
\]
Indeed, \(c_1\) is the area of \(K\cap\{f_1\leq0\}\), and the two closed halfplane sections overlap only on the null cutting line \(\{f_1=0\}\). Substituting the displayed formula for \(c_1\) and using (5) proves (7).

We next prove the centroid localization with the closed side of the cut. The exact cells whose indices contain \(1\) partition
\[
C_1:=A_2\cap\{f_1\leq-L_1\}.
\]
Under all-double support their total area is
\[
q_{123}+q_{12}+q_{13}
=q+x_3+x_2
=m-x_1.
\]
Thus (3) gives (10). Notice that the cutting line \(f_1=-L_1\) belongs to this closed complementary cap. Hence, if \(g_2\) were either in its interior or on its boundary, \(C_1\) would be a closed halfplane section of \(A_2\) containing \(g_2\). The planar Grünbaum inequality recorded in accepted fact `2f9be517307232c7` would give
\[
|C_1|\geq\frac{4m}{9},
\]
contrary to (10). Therefore
\[
f_1(g_2)>-L_1.
\tag{15}
\]

For completeness, \(g_2\in\operatorname{int}A_2\). Otherwise a supporting affine functional nonnegative on \(A_2\) and zero at \(g_2\) would be strictly positive on a positive-area subset of the two-dimensional body \(A_2\), contradicting that its integral equals its value at the centroid times \(m\).

Put
\[
\phi_i=f_i+L_i.
\]
Then \(\phi_1(g_2)>0\) by (15), while
\[
\phi_1+\phi_2+\phi_3=-1+L_1+L_2+L_3<0.
\tag{16}
\]
Suppose \(\phi_2(g_2)>0\). Equation (16) gives \(\phi_3(g_2)<0\). Since all three signs are then strict and \(g_2\in\operatorname{int}A_2\), a neighborhood of \(g_2\) in \(A_2\) lies in the exact chamber \(Q_3\), giving \(q_3>0\), contrary to the stated positive support. If instead \(\phi_2(g_2)=0\), then (16) again gives \(\phi_3(g_2)<0\). The function \(\phi_2\) is nonconstant, so a sufficiently small half-disk about the interior point \(g_2\), on the side \(\phi_2>0\), still has \(\phi_1>0\) and \(\phi_3<0\). It lies in \(Q_3\) and has positive area, giving the same contradiction. Hence
\[
\phi_2(g_2)<0.
\]
The identical argument with \(2\) and \(3\) exchanged gives
\[
\phi_3(g_2)<0.
\]
Together with (15), these are exactly (8), and they place \(g_2\) in the strict interior of (9).

The one-cut open cap \(A_2\cap\{\phi_1>0\}\) is the disjoint union of the exact cells whose indices omit \(1\), namely \(Q_\varnothing,Q_2,Q_3,Q_{23}\). The first is forced empty. In \(Q_2\), the inequalities \(\phi_1>0\) and \(\phi_3>0\), together with (16), force \(\phi_2<0\), so \(Q_2\) is the intersection of \(A_2\) with an open ambient chamber. If it were nonempty, that open chamber would meet \(\operatorname{int}A_2\): from any point of the intersection, move a sufficiently small distance toward an interior point of \(A_2\). The intersection would then have positive area, contrary to \(q_2=0\). Hence \(Q_2=\varnothing\). The same argument gives \(Q_3=\varnothing\). Therefore
\[
A_2\cap\{\phi_1>0\}=Q_{23}
\]
as an exact set, and its area is \(x_1\). The boundary \(\phi_1=0\) is assigned to cells whose indices contain \(1\), exactly as used in (10).

It remains to verify (11). In the all-double case, the exact identity of accepted fact `91cb5bfc71da49ac` is
\[
W=3(U+m+q+E_R)-(2M-m-k).
\]
Since \(W=0\),
\[
2M=m+k+3(U+m+q+E_R).
\tag{17}
\]
The strict actual-counterexample balance (2) gives \(2M<2m+2k\). Combining this with (17) and rearranging yields
\[
k>2m+3q+3U+3E_R.
\]
Here \(U\geq0\), while \(E_R>0\) because \(r_{123}>0\). This proves both inequalities in (11). The canonical tails at index \(1\) add no independent restriction: after the crossing identity they reduce to \(t_1\geq0\) and \(t_1\geq m-M\), both weaker than (5) under \(M\geq m\).
statement:
Let \(N=\{1,2,3\}\), and assume the complete canonical finite-interior common-plane hypotheses and exact-cell convention of accepted fact `0e51a47a9add571f`. Write
\[
M=|A_0|,\qquad m=|A_2|,\qquad k=|K|,
\qquad h=\frac{2(M+m+k)}9,
\]
and use the notation of accepted fact `91cb5bfc71da49ac`:
\[
u_i=\sum_{J\ni i}p_J,\qquad
v_i=\sum_{H\ni i}q_H,\qquad
c_i=\sum_{G\ni i}r_G.
\]
Assume \(M\geq m\), the three crossings and canonical tails
\[
u_i+v_i+c_i=h,\qquad
c_i+m\geq h,\qquad c_i+M\geq h,
\]
and
\[
W=0.
\]
Suppose the positive \(Q\)-support is exactly
\[
\{123,12,13,23\},
\]
put
\[
q=q_{123}>0,\qquad
x_i=q_{N\setminus\{i\}}>0,\qquad
m=q+x_1+x_2+x_3,
\]
and assume
\[
r_1r_2r_3r_{123}>0.
\]
Suppose, finally, that the full three-slice realization is an actual canonical counterexample, rather than merely a point in its closure.

Accepted fact `aee01fb887f2b3bd`, with its Scott calculation kept before discarding the nonnegative \(u_i\), gives
\[
M+m-k\geq\frac92\min_{i\in N}(u_i+m-x_i).
\tag{1}
\]
Accepted fact `2f9be517307232c7` gives the strict large-slice necessary condition
\[
M<m+k.
\tag{2}
\]

There is a unique index \(i\) for which \(x_i>5m/9\). Relabeling this index as \(1\), one has
\[
x_1>\frac{5m}{9},
\qquad
q+x_2+x_3=m-x_1<\frac{4m}{9},
\qquad
\max\{x_2,x_3\}<\frac{4m}{9}.
\tag{3}
\]
Moreover, \(i=1\) is the unique minimizer in (1), equivalently the unique minimizer of
\[
|K\cap\{f_i\geq0\}|=k-h+u_i+m-x_i.
\]
It satisfies
\[
u_1<x_1-\frac{5m}{9}.
\tag{4}
\]
Thus, for
\[
t_1:=x_1-u_1,
\]
one has
\[
t_1>\frac{5m}{9},
\tag{5}
\]
\[
c_1=h-m+t_1>h-\frac{4m}{9},
\tag{6}
\]
and, with the cutting line assigned exactly as in the canonical cells,
\[
\left|K\cap\{f_1\geq0\}\right|
=k-c_1
=k-h+m-t_1
<k-h+\frac{4m}{9}.
\tag{7}
\]

Let
\[
g_2=\frac1m\int_{A_2}z\,dz
\]
be the centroid of \(A_2\). Then
\[
f_1(g_2)>-L_1,\qquad
f_2(g_2)<-L_2,\qquad
f_3(g_2)<-L_3,
\tag{8}
\]
so \(g_2\) lies in the strict interior of the dominant exact cell
\[
Q_{23}
=A_2\cap\{f_1>-L_1,\ f_2\leq-L_2,\ f_3\leq-L_3\}.
\tag{9}
\]
The one-cut open cap \(A_2\cap\{f_1>-L_1\}\) has area \(x_1\), while its complementary closed cap has area
\[
\left|A_2\cap\{f_1\leq-L_1\}\right|
=m-x_1<\frac{4m}{9}.
\tag{10}
\]
With the exact weak/strict convention, the inactive cells \(Q_\varnothing,Q_2,Q_3\) are empty, not merely null. Hence the literal set equality
\[
Q_{23}=A_2\cap\{f_1>-L_1\}
\]
holds, while the cutting line \(f_1=-L_1\) belongs to the complementary closed cap in (10).

Finally, put
\[
U=\sum_i u_i,\qquad
E_R=\sum_{|G|=2}r_G+2r_{123}.
\]
The hypotheses also imply the additional exact strict scalar inequality
\[
k>2m+3q+3U+3E_R>2m+3q.
\tag{11}
\]
